summary: This informational document discusses options and requirements for rendering RFCs as PDF, as outlined in RFC 6949. It also covers the use of PDF for Internet-Drafts and the software tools available or needed for producing and working with PDF.

plainLanguage.summary: This talks about how to produce print-friendly PDF copies of RFCs and what tools are needed.

subtitle: Options and recommendations for rendering RFCs and Internet-Drafts as PDF files.

tldr.problem: PDF covers a wide range of capabilities, so two PDFs that look alike can differ greatly in archivability, accessibility, searchability and embedded content.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends PDF 1.7 with PDF/A-3 conformance level U for RFCs, PDF/UA for accessibility, A4 pages, embedded fonts, active hyperlinks, XMP metadata and the XML source embedded in the file.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational, its details were expected to change as the publication toolsets were completed, and it is updated by RFC 9920.

today: RFC 7995 is an Informational document and is updated by RFC 9920. Its details were expected to change as the publication toolsets were completed.

sections.title: Why PDF Needs Rules
sections.content:
Future RFCs use XML as the canonical format, with renderings in several formats including PDF (see RFC 6949). Because PDF has such a wide range of capabilities, not all PDFs are equal. Visually similar documents could be scanned or rasterized images, or could include text layout options, hyperlinks, embedded fonts and digital signatures.

RFC 7995 explains the options and makes recommendations for both RFCs and Internet-Drafts. It also notes that PDF is less well known in the IETF community than the other RFC formats, and it expects its details to change as the new toolsets are implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: Two PDFs can look the same but behave very differently, like a photo of a book page versus real text. These rules say which kind to make.

sections.title: Choosing PDF Versions and Standards
sections.content:
Newer PDF versions add features, while older versions are supported by more legacy viewers. Beyond the base format there are application standards: PDF/X for prepress exchange and PDF/E for engineering documents. Two families matter most for RFCs: PDF/A for long-term preservation and PDF/UA for accessibility.

The recommendations are:

  • Use PDF 1.7, which is well supported by widely available viewers.
  • For RFCs, require PDF/A-3 with conformance level U, which adds mandatory Unicode mapping.
  • Use PDF/A-3 for embedding additional data, including the XML source file.
  • Use PDF/UA for user accessibility.
sections.plainLanguage: There are special grades of PDF: one built to last for many years and one built so screen readers can use it. The RFCs pick both.

sections.title: How the PDF Should Look
sections.content:
The "visible" recommendations cover what a reader sees. The Internet-Draft and RFC processors should produce A4 by default, using portrait mode with left and right margins of 20 mm and top and bottom margins of 33 mm, so the page prints well on both A4 and US Letter without scaling.

Headers and footers should be unobtrusive, placed so they do not interfere with screen readers, and carry the RFC number or draft name, page number, category, shortened author names, date and short title. When the XML editing=yes option is chosen, paragraph numbers go in the right margin so they are not confused with section numbers.

All fonts should be embedded, since PDF/A mandates it, and typeface choices should follow the HTML and CSS rendering recommendations (RFC 7992, RFC 7993). Mid-word hyphenated line breaks should be avoided, because they can be harmful inside protocol elements. All hyperlinks in the HTML rendition should be active in the PDF, and the PDF should look like the HTML rendition at least in spirit, with page numbers in the table of contents and running headers and footers as the main differences.
sections.plainLanguage: The PDF should be a clean, good-looking page that prints well on any paper, with fonts built in so it looks the same everywhere and links that really work.

sections.title: The Invisible Features
sections.content:
The "invisible" recommendations make the PDF useful to software and to people using assistive tools.

  • Text order: text in content streams should follow the XML document's logical order, which supports searching, annotation and text-to-speech. PDF/UA requires this.
  • Unicode: generated PDFs must contain the full text as it appears in the XML. Unicode normalization may occur.
  • Artwork: if both ASCII art and SVG exist for a picture, prefer the SVG. ASCII artwork must use a monospace font.
  • Alt-text: alt-text for artwork and figures should be stored in the PDF /Alt property.
  • Metadata: all metadata from the XML, including author, date, series and a retrieval URL, should be embedded as XMP metadata, consistent with the RFC Editor info page.
  • Structure: section structure should map to PDF document structure so reader bookmarks work, ideally with the same fragment identifiers as the HTML version.
  • Embedded files: embed the XML source and all illustrations for RFCs, make this standard for Internet-Drafts if possible, and embed named <sourcecode> entries and bitmap images.
sections.plainLanguage: Behind the scenes the PDF keeps real text in the right order, descriptions of pictures, facts about the document, and even the original source file tucked inside.

sections.title: Signatures and Security
sections.content:
Digital signatures can show that an RFC is the original and unmodified. Signatures also cover embedded content, so embedding the XML source lets the source be signed too. The signing method is left to separate policy. If signatures are used, the authors suggest that PDFs generated by the Internet-Draft upload tools be signed with no restrictions on later changes, while PDFs generated by the RFC Editor be signed and certified, with restrictions allowing only additional signatures and comments.

The security section lists threats: user-submitted PDF Internet-Drafts might carry malware aimed at PDF readers, printers or validation tools, and the PDF production toolset might itself be tricked into producing malware-bearing files. The specification aims to avoid features such as scripting. Mitigations are careful security reviews of the toolsets and careful examination of any submitted PDFs.
sections.plainLanguage: A digital signature is like a wax seal showing nobody changed the document. The main danger is that a bad PDF could carry a computer virus, so the tools must be checked carefully.
